title: Lesson 67 - There Has to Be a Balance

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: The fixed-day model gives you Tuesday and Wednesday from nine to four, a monthly fee and no requests on the other three weekdays. That sounds predictable.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: It is predictable, although two full days could make deadlines for existing clients bunch together on Monday and Thursday.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: The flexible model gives you sixty hours a month, mostly remote, with at least forty-eight hours’ notice for meetings.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: That protects location choice, but the hours could spread across every week. There has to be a balance between flexibility on paper and being mentally available all the time.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: What are you actually trying to protect?

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: I need two uninterrupted design blocks each week so that complex work doesn’t get divided into tiny pieces. I also need evenings that are not treated as emergency capacity.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: The reason you prefer protected blocks is that switching between projects costs attention, not just minutes.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: Exactly. Even though the flexible model looks easier to fit around current work, it could create more switching if meetings move every week.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Could a monthly cap solve that?

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: Only partly. In order to make the cap meaningful, I’d have to know whether messages, revisions and internal meetings all count toward the sixty hours.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: What would make the fixed-day model workable?

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: A review after six weeks, permission to protect two existing client commitments, and a rule that unused hours don’t become evening requests. The trade-off is less weekday flexibility in exchange for clearer boundaries.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: And the flexible model?

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: I would need two defined availability windows and a weekly hour ceiling so that “flexible” didn’t mean “always reachable.” The trade-off is more scheduling freedom but more coordination.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Which arrangement better supports the values you ranked yesterday?

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: The fixed days support predictability and recovery better, while the flexible hours protect location choice. Although creative exchange matters, it won’t be sustainable if I arrive at every shared review already overloaded.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: So the purpose of a trial would be to test the workload pattern, not to prove that collective work suits you forever.

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: Yes. Looking back at my workspace experiment, what helped was a clear review point and no automatic continuation. I’d use the same principle here without assuming the two situations are identical.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: What will you propose?

lines.speaker: Aisha
lines.text: I’ll ask whether the fixed-day model could be tested for six weeks within the larger six-month discussion, with written scope, counted hours and an exit review. That is a question, not an acceptance.
